hints: Focus on what counts as an organic anion here, a carbon-containing negative ion like a carboxylate $\text{RCOO}^-$ or alkoxide $\text{RO}^-$.
Recall the two different hydrolysis routes for nitriles: alkaline hydrolysis gives the carboxylate salt plus ammonia, while acid hydrolysis gives the neutral carboxylic acid.
Check the other two starting materials for acidity: alkanes and alcohols are far too weakly acidic to be deprotonated by dilute $\text{NaOH}$ in good yield.
walkthrough:
**Define the target**

Think organic anion means the negative charge stays on a carbon-containing species.

Good examples are $\text{CH}_3\text{COO}^-$ (ethanoate) and $\text{C}_2\text{H}_5\text{O}^-$ (ethoxide).

**Recall nitrile hydrolysis**

Ethanenitrile, $\text{CH}_3\text{CN}$, is hydrolysed on heating under reflux.

The conditions decide the organic product:
$$\text{CH}_3\text{CN} + \text{H}^+ / \text{H}_2\text{O} \rightarrow \text{CH}_3\text{COOH}$$
$$\text{CH}_3\text{CN} + \text{OH}^- / \text{H}_2\text{O} \rightarrow \text{CH}_3\text{COO}^- + \text{NH}_3$$

**Apply to options A and B**

With dilute $\text{NaOH}$, you get sodium ethanoate, which contains the anion $\text{CH}_3\text{COO}^-$ in good yield.

With dilute $\text{H}_2\text{SO}_4$, you get neutral ethanoic acid, $\text{CH}_3\text{COOH}$, not an anion.

**Rule out C and D**

Ethane, $\text{C}_2\text{H}_6$, is an unreactive alkane and does not react with $\text{Na}$ metal.

Ethanol, $\text{C}_2\text{H}_5\text{OH}$, is a weaker acid than water, so dilute $\text{NaOH}$ cannot deprotonate it to $\text{C}_2\text{H}_5\text{O}^-$ in good yield. Only reactive $\text{Na}$ metal would do that.

options.A: Alkaline hydrolysis of ethanenitrile gives sodium ethanoate and ammonia: $\text{CH}_3\text{CN} + \text{NaOH} + \text{H}_2\text{O} \rightarrow \text{CH}_3\text{COO}^-\text{Na}^+ + \text{NH}_3$. The organic product is the ethanoate anion in good yield, exactly what is asked for.
options.B: Acid hydrolysis of ethanenitrile gives the neutral carboxylic acid: $\text{CH}_3\text{CN} + 2\text{H}_2\text{O} + \text{H}^+ \rightarrow \text{CH}_3\text{COOH} + \text{NH}_4^+$. Although $\text{NH}_4^+$ is an ion, it is inorganic, and the organic product is uncharged.
options.C: Ethane is a very unreactive alkane with strong C-H and C-C bonds and no acidic proton. It does not react with sodium metal, so no ethide anion or other organic anion forms. Students sometimes confuse alkanes with alkynes, which are acidic enough to react with Na.
options.D: Ethanol is only very weakly acidic ($K_a$ much smaller than water), so the equilibrium $\text{C}_2\text{H}_5\text{OH} + \text{OH}^- \rightleftharpoons \text{C}_2\text{H}_5\text{O}^- + \text{H}_2\text{O}$ lies far to the left. No good yield of ethoxide forms. The trap is thinking any acid plus alkali makes a salt, but alcohols need Na metal, not NaOH.
